title: There are people who spend their entire lives trying to outrun a name they never chose.
paragraphs: There are people who spend their entire lives trying to outrun a name they never chose.

Some were named by angry fathers.
Some were labeled by disappointed mothers.
Some were defined by rumors, failures, addictions, betrayals, trauma, divorce papers, abandoned childhoods, secret sins, or the worst moment of their lives.
And eventually… the label starts sounding more believable than the voice of God.
That is where the story of Jabez begins.

Not with victory.
Not with blessing.
Not with greatness.
But with pain.
Hidden quietly inside a genealogy most people skip over while reading Scripture is one of the most emotionally devastating introductions in the entire Bible.
The Bible says:

“And Jabez was more honorable than his brethren: and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, Because I bare him with sorrow.”
— 1 Chronicles 4:9 (KJV)

At first glance, it feels small.
Almost forgettable.
But the original Hebrew opens the wound deeper.
The name “Jabez” comes from the Hebrew:
יַעְבֵּץ — Yaʿbēṣ
Derived from the Hebrew root:
עָצַב — atsab

Which means:
pain,
grief,
sorrow,
anguish,
emotional torment,
to hurt deeply,
to labor in agony.
This is the same root connected to emotional suffering and painful toil throughout the Old Testament.
His own mother looked at him… and named him Pain.

Not “joy.”
Not “promise.”
Not “hope.”
Pain.
Imagine growing up hearing your identity spoken over you every single day.

“Come here, Pain.”
“Pain, help your brothers.”
“Pain, where are you?”
“Pain, why are you like this?”
Some people reading this understand that feeling more than they want to admit.

Because maybe nobody called you “Jabez,” but they called you:
mistake,
failure,
disappointment,
too broken,
too emotional,
too sinful,
too damaged,
too weak,
too late,
too far gone.

And after years of hearing it…
you started agreeing with it.
But the most shocking part of Jabez’s story is not what his mother called him.
It is what God called him afterward.
Because Heaven did not agree with the label placed on his life.
The Scripture says:

“And Jabez was more honorable than his brethren…”
— 1 Chronicles 4:9
The Hebrew word for “honorable” is:
כָּבֵד — kāḇēḏ

Meaning:
weighty,
significant,
full of substance,
worthy of honor,
glorious.
The boy named Pain became weighty in the eyes of God.
Do not miss this.
The very person expected to become a symbol of sorrow became marked by honor instead.
This is the Gospel hidden inside a genealogy.
God specializes in rewriting identities.

Abram became Abraham.
Jacob became Israel.
Simon became Peter.
Saul became Paul.
And broken people still become new creations through Jesus Christ today.
The enemy wants labels to become prisons.
But God uses grace to become resurrection.
Then comes the prayer.
One of the most powerful cries in all of Scripture is only a few lines long, but it carries the desperation of a wounded soul refusing to stay chained to inherited pain.
Jabez prayed:

“Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me!”
— 1 Chronicles 4:10 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the phrase “bless me indeed” carries intense emphasis.
בָּרֵךְ תְּבָרֲכֵנִי — bārek tebārekēnī

Literally:
“Blessing, bless me.”
“Surely bless me.”
“Overflow me with blessing.”
This was not greed.
This was survival.
Jabez was praying against a destiny everyone assumed he would fulfill.
He was saying:
“Lord… do not let my pain become my future.”

Some people inherit generational anger.
Others inherit addiction.
Others inherit abandonment.
Others inherit spiritual darkness.
Others inherit cycles nobody talks about publicly.
Jabez understood something most people miss:
Pain repeats itself unless God interrupts it.
And then he says:
“Enlarge my coast…”
Hebrew:
הַרְבִּיתָ אֶת־גְּבוּלִי — harbīta et-gevūlī

Meaning:
expand my boundaries,
increase my territory,
make room for more.
But this was never just about land.

This was about influence.
Purpose.
Calling.
Capacity.
A man born under sorrow was asking God for more room than his pain allowed him to imagine.
That hits differently when you realize how many believers still live imprisoned inside old wounds.
There are Christians who love Jesus deeply but still secretly believe they are disqualified from being used by God because of what happened to them.
But Jabez teaches something dangerous to hopelessness:
Your beginning does not own your ending.
Then comes the line that destroys me every time I read it.
“That thine hand might be with me…”

The “hand” of God throughout Scripture symbolizes:
favor,
guidance,
protection,
authority,
presence,
power.
Jabez was not merely asking for things.
He was asking for God Himself.
Because healed people eventually realize something wounded people often miss:
No blessing on earth can replace the presence of God.
Moses understood this when he said:

“If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence.”
— Exodus 33:15
David understood it after his sin when he cried:

“Cast me not away from thy presence.”
— Psalm 51:11
And Jabez understood it too.

Because people who have truly suffered know that money cannot heal emptiness.
Success cannot resurrect dead peace.
Applause cannot remove shame.
Only God can touch the places nobody else can reach.
And then comes the final part of the prayer.
“Keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me.”
The Hebrew implication is profound.
Jabez is essentially praying:
“Do not allow evil to produce the same pain my name carries.”
He was asking God to stop the cycle.

This is not just a prayer.
This is spiritual warfare against inherited destruction.
And then Scripture closes the entire story with one terrifyingly beautiful sentence:

“And God granted him that which he requested.”
— 1 Chronicles 4:10
That is it.

No dramatic buildup.
No long explanation.
Just four words that change everything.
God granted him.
The boy named Pain was heard by Heaven.
Do you understand what this means?
God listened to the prayer of someone society would have overlooked inside a genealogy nobody pays attention to.
Because God has always specialized in finding hidden people carrying silent pain.

Hagar in the wilderness.
Joseph in prison.
David in the fields.
Mary in obscurity.
Peter after failure.
Thomas in doubt.
The woman with the issue of blood.
The thief on the cross.

And maybe…
you.
The world may know your wound before it knows your heart.
But God sees deeper than labels.
This is why the Gospel of Jesus Christ changes everything.
Because Jesus Himself carried sorrow publicly.
The prophet Isaiah wrote:

“He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
— Isaiah 53:3
In Hebrew:
מַכְאֹבוֹת — makʾōḇōṯ

Sorrows.
Pains.
Sufferings.
Jesus entered human pain willingly so broken people could receive new names.

Through Christ:
the guilty become forgiven,
the orphan becomes adopted,
the addict becomes restored,
the ashamed become cleansed,
the dead become alive.
The cross was the greatest identity exchange in human history.
And maybe that is why the story of Jabez still wrecks people emotionally thousands of years later.

Because deep down…
everyone knows what it feels like to carry a name they are trying to escape.

Some are trying to outrun childhood wounds.
Some are hiding addictions.
Some smile publicly while bleeding privately.
Some sit in church every Sunday secretly convinced God could never fully use them.
But Jabez stands inside Scripture like living proof that pain does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
And maybe tonight somebody needs to pray the prayer they have been too afraid to pray.

“Lord…
rewrite what pain tried to name.”

Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
The name pain gave you is not the name Heaven plans to finish with.
